items.stem: Define the term 'business plan'.
items.answer: A document describing a business, its objectives and strategies, the market it operates in and its financial forecasts, often used to obtain finance.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a document describing a business, its objectives and strategies, the market it operates in and its financial forecasts, often used to obtain finance. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two benefits to a business of having a corporate plan.
items.answer: It gives clear direction and coordinates departments; it helps allocate resources to priorities; it provides a benchmark to monitor performance.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark benefit, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a business plan may help a business obtain a bank loan.
items.answer: It shows the bank the objectives, market research, cash-flow and profit forecasts, reassuring it that the loan can be repaid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark contents; 1 mark reassurance of repayment. [2]

items.stem: Based in Dubai, Desert Bloom Hotels plc (public limited company) operates fourteen four- and five-star hotels. The business has around 3,100 employees. Occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby. Explain how a corporate plan could help Desert Bloom achieve its long-term objectives.
items.answer: Points to develop for Desert Bloom: corporate plan sets objectives, strategies and resources; coordinates functional plans; allocates finance to priorities; allows monitoring and review.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: corporate plan sets objectives, strategies and resources. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Desert Bloom: hospitality, about 3,100 employees, public limited company in the United Arab Emirates; occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Desert Bloom, e.g. coordinates functional plans; allocates finance to priorities; allows monitoring and review. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: A major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six. Mekong Furniture JSC, a joint stock company in Vietnam with about 1,200 employees, makes wooden and rattan furniture for large retailers in the USA and Europe. Discuss whether Mekong Furniture should rely on planned strategy or allow strategy to emerge.
items.answer: For: planned strategy gives clarity; coordinates resources; reassures investors. Against: emergent strategy responds to change; plans may fail; learning from experience. Judgement: the decision for Mekong Furniture depends mainly on market volatility, and also on management style.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Mekong Furniture, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Define the term 'corporate culture'.
items.answer: The values, attitudes, beliefs and ways of behaving shared by people in an organisation ("the way we do things around here").
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, the values, attitudes, beliefs and ways of behaving shared by people in an organisation ("the way we do things around here"). 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how corporate culture can influence a firm's strategy.
items.answer: Culture shapes attitudes to risk and change; an innovative culture supports new products, while a risk-averse role culture favours cautious strategies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark culture shapes attitudes; 1 mark effect on strategic choice. [2]

items.stem: Explain why culture clashes are a common problem after mergers.
items.answer: The two firms have different values, management styles and ways of working, which cause conflict, low morale and poor integration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark different values; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Lumen Robotics: culture = shared values and behaviour; innovative culture supports new products such as robots for hospital logistics; risk-averse culture slows change; culture affects motivation and recruitment.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: culture = shared values and behaviour. items.stem: Define the term 'change management'.
items.answer: Planning, implementing and controlling changes in an organisation so that they are accepted and achieve their objectives.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, planning, implementing and controlling changes in an organisation so that they are accepted and achieve their objectives. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why employees may resist change.
items.answer: Fear of job losses or lower pay; loss of status or skills; fear of the unknown; poor communication and lack of trust.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why "anchoring the change in the culture" is the final step in Kotter's model.
items.answer: Unless new behaviours become part of the shared values, staff drift back to old habits once pressure eases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark embed in culture; 1 mark prevent reversion. [2]

items.stem: What is the first of Kotter's eight steps for leading change?
options: Anchor the change in the culture
items.answer: Create a sense of urgency
items.markingKey: Create a sense of urgency. People must first see why change is needed.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'resistance to change'?
options: Unwillingness of employees or managers to accept change, often because of fear of the unknown, job loss, loss of status or poor communication.
A long-term plan for the whole organisation, setting out its objectives and the strategies and resources needed to achieve them.
A culture in which power is concentrated in one person or a small group at the centre, who make quick decisions.
Preparing in advance for unexpected events, by identifying possible risks and deciding the actions and resources needed to deal with them.
items.answer: Unwillingness of employees or managers to accept change, often because of fear of the unknown, job loss, loss of status or poor communication.
items.markingKey: resistance to change: Unwillingness of employees or managers to accept change, often because of fear of the unknown, job loss, loss of status or poor communication.

items.stem: Explain how communication can reduce resistance to change.
items.answer: Explaining why change is needed, how it will affect staff and listening to concerns reduces uncertainty and rumours and builds trust.
items.markingKey: 1 mark explain reasons/effects; 1 mark reduces fear/builds trust. [2]

items.answer: A → C → B

items.stem: Define the term 'crisis management'.
items.answer: Responding to a sudden, unexpected event that threatens the business, its reputation or stakeholders, in a way that limits the damage.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, responding to a sudden, unexpected event that threatens the business, its reputation or stakeholders, in a way that limits the damage. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why contingency planning can be expensive yet worthwhile.
items.answer: It requires time, training, backup systems and spare resources that may never be used, but it greatly reduces losses and recovery time if a crisis happens.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cost; 1 mark benefit in a crisis. [2]

items.stem: Explain two features of effective crisis management.
items.answer: Fast decision-making by a crisis team; clear, honest communication with stakeholders; rapid action to protect people and restore operations.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark feature, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.answer: Some events are unforeseeable and resources are limited, so planning focuses on the most likely and most damaging risks.

items.stem: Lanka Tea Estates plc has identified two risks — a fire at the main site: probability 0.02 a year, cost $1,000k; a cyber-attack on its IT systems: probability 0.15 a year, cost $150k. Calculate the expected annual cost of each risk. A contingency plan costing $30k a year would cut the probability of the first risk by 50%. Calculate whether the plan is financially worthwhile.
